# Isochronic Passage Chart

> An interactive globe showing expected door-to-door travel time from each of 553
> origin cities to every land area on Earth, combining scheduled air routes,
> rail from OpenStreetMap route relations, ferry crossings, and a road-speed model
> calibrated against 2,998 real driving journeys, with check-in, border-control
> and transfer penalties. Air times are fitted to 107,366 ADS-B flight legs.
> Named after Francis Galton's "Isochronic Passage Chart for Travellers" (1881),
> the first published travel-time map.

## What the numbers mean

Times are expected door-to-door minutes, rendered in 11 bands from under 2 hours
to over 72 hours. A departure is treated as planned, so the first service is not
waited for; onward connections are, because a traveller cannot choose when a
connecting service leaves. Waiting is derived from route frequency, which is why
remote islands correctly resolve to days rather than hours.

## How it is computed

A single-source Dijkstra runs over one multi-modal graph per origin city:
548,557 H3 resolution-5 land cells (about 253 km2 each), plus a departure and an
arrival node for each of 3,983 airports with scheduled passenger service.
Ground movement between adjacent cells is charged at a per-cell speed derived
from GRIP4 road-density rasters. Flights connect airport pairs taken from
Wikipedia's "Airlines and destinations" tables, resolved to IATA codes through
Wikidata property P238, with block time modelled from great-circle distance.

## Known limits

- Rail and ferry are not yet in the graph.
- Flight frequency is a fitted gravity model, not published timetables.
- Coverage is about 98% of land; the remainder has no modelled route.

## Data sources

- OurAirports (public domain) — airport locations and service status
- Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0) — airline route network
- Wikidata (CC0) — IATA code resolution
- OpenStreetMap (ODbL) — coastlines drawn on the map; rail route relations
- GRIP4 (CC0) — global road density
- Natural Earth (public domain) — land mask, lakes, borders, place names

## Links

- Chart: https://worldmap.atik.kr/
- Machine-readable index: https://worldmap.atik.kr/index.json

## Disclaimer

For reference only. All figures are estimates computed from open data and a simplified model. They carry no warranty of accuracy, are not travel advice, and must not be relied on for any journey, booking, or decision. The author accepts no liability for any use.

## Grid and geometry (2026-09-10)

- H3 resolution 6 (5.6 km across) everywhere, refined to resolution 7 (2.1 km) where roads reach secondary grade or a metropolitan area lies (East Asia, South Asia, Europe, North America and every other built-up region).
- Hexagons are drawn unrounded; bands are emitted at four levels of detail so no gap can open at any zoom.
- Coastlines: OpenStreetMap water polygons at zoom 12 (~10 m). Lakes: HydroLAKES (CC BY 4.0).
- Place names under the cursor: GeoNames cities15000 (CC BY 4.0). Address search and click-to-address: OpenStreetMap Nominatim; queries are sent to nominatim.openstreetmap.org only when typed or clicked.
- Rail legs name the station and line (OpenStreetMap route relations).
